result.statement: If there be two straight lines, and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A and BC be the two straight lines, and let BC be cut at random at the points D and E, so that BC is divided into the segments BD, DE, EC. (Two points of section are taken for definiteness; the argument below is the same for any number of points, one further parallel being drawn for each additional point of section.) It is required to prove that the rectangle contained by A, BC is equal to the rectangles contained by A, BD; by A, DE; and by A, EC together.

**Step 2.** From the point B draw BF at right angles to BC [1.11], so that the angle FBC is right.

**Step 3.** From BF cut off BG equal to A [1.3].

**Step 4.** Through G draw GH parallel to BC [1.31]; and through D, E, C draw DK, EL, CH parallel to BG [1.31], meeting GH at the points K, L, H respectively.

**Step 5.** Since DK, EL, CH are each parallel to BG, they are also parallel to one another [1.30]. Hence each of the figures BK, BL, BH, DL, EH is a parallelogram: its two sides lying along GH and BC are parallel (Step 4), and its two remaining sides are two of the parallels BG, DK, EL, CH.

**Step 6.** A parallelogram having one right angle has all its angles right. For each side of the parallelogram is a straight line falling upon the two parallels that form the adjacent sides, so that the two interior angles on the same side of it together equal two right angles [1.29]; hence each angle adjacent to the right angle is right, and, applying the same reasoning again, so is the angle opposite. Such a parallelogram is rectangular, and is the rectangle contained by the two straight lines about its right angle [D2.1].

**Step 7.** The angle GBC is right (Step 2), and it is an angle of the parallelogram BH; therefore BH is a rectangular parallelogram (Step 6). It is contained by GB, BC, which contain the right angle GBC; and GB is equal to A (Step 3). Therefore BH is the rectangle contained by A, BC [D2.1].

**Step 8.** The angle GBD is the same right angle GBC, and it is an angle of the parallelogram BK; therefore BK is rectangular (Step 6), contained by GB, BD, and GB is equal to A. Therefore BK is the rectangle contained by A, BD [D2.1].

**Step 9.** Since BC falls upon the parallels BG, DK, the exterior angle KDE is equal to the interior and opposite angle GBD [1.29]; but GBD is right, so KDE is right, and DL is a rectangular parallelogram (Step 6) contained by DK, DE. Now in the parallelogram BK the opposite sides BG, DK are equal [1.34]; and BG is equal to A; therefore DK is equal to A [CN1]. Therefore DL is the rectangle contained by A, DE [D2.1].

**Step 10.** In the same way, since BC falls upon the parallels BG, EL, the exterior angle LEC is equal to the interior and opposite angle GBE [1.29], which is right; so EH is a rectangular parallelogram (Step 6) contained by EL, EC. In the parallelogram BL the opposite sides BG, EL are equal [1.34]; and BG is equal to A; therefore EL is equal to A [CN1]. Therefore EH is the rectangle contained by A, EC [D2.1].

**Step 11.** The straight lines DK, EL divide the rectangle BH into the three rectangles BK, DL, EH, and no part of BH lies outside them; therefore BH is equal to BK, DL, EH taken together, the whole being made up of its parts.

**Step 12.** Substituting the descriptions obtained in Steps 7–10: the rectangle contained by A, BC (which is BH) is equal to the rectangle contained by A, BD (which is BK), together with the rectangle contained by A, DE (which is DL) and the rectangle contained by A, EC (which is EH). For any number of points of section the same construction yields one rectangle for each segment, each contained by a straight line equal to A and that segment, and their sum is again the whole rectangle BH.

Therefore, if there be two straight lines and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments. Q.E.D.

Path note: the auxiliary lines DK, EL, CH were drawn as parallels to BG [1.31] rather than as perpendiculars to BC [1.11], since parallels give the parallelogram structure needed for 1.34 directly, and their right angles then follow from 1.29 in one step.

result.statement: If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and both of the segments is equal to the square on the whole.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut at random at the point C. It is required to prove that the rectangle contained by AB, AC together with the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the square on AB.

**Step 2.** On AB describe the square ADEB [1.46], with the vertex D adjoining A and the vertex E adjoining B. By the construction of 1.46, the side DE is drawn parallel to AB and the side BE parallel to AD.

**Step 3.** Through C draw CF parallel to AD [1.31], and let it meet DE at F. The straight line CF divides the square AE into the two quadrilaterals AF (that is, ACFD) and CE (that is, CBEF); thus the square AE is made up of the figures AF and CE.

**Step 4.** AF is a parallelogram, for AD is parallel to CF by construction, and AC, DF are parts of the parallel sides AB, DE of the square. Its angles at A and D are angles of the square ADEB and are therefore right [D1.22]; hence its opposite angles at F and at C are also right [1.34], so that AF is a rectangular parallelogram. By D2.1 it is the rectangle contained by DA, AC; and since DA is equal to AB, being sides of the square [D1.22], AF is the rectangle contained by AB, AC.

**Step 5.** In the same way CE is a parallelogram, for CF is parallel to BE by construction, and CB, FE are parts of the parallel sides AB, DE. Its angles at B and E are angles of the square and are right [D1.22]; hence its opposite angles at F and at C are right [1.34], and CE is a rectangular parallelogram. By D2.1 it is the rectangle contained by BE, BC; and since BE is equal to AB [D1.22], CE is the rectangle contained by AB, BC.

**Step 6.** AE is the square on AB, by the construction of Step 2.

**Step 7.** Therefore, since the square AE is made up of AF and CE, the square on AB is equal to the rectangle contained by AB, AC together with the rectangle contained by AB, BC. That is, if a straight line AB is cut at random at C, the rectangles contained by the whole AB and each of the segments AC, CB together equal the square on AB. Q.E.D.

Path note: the result could also be derived from Proposition 2.1 by taking the uncut line equal to AB, but that route needs an extra lemma identifying the rectangle contained by two lines equal to AB with the square on AB; the direct division of the square is chosen because the statement itself concerns the square on AB, which this construction exhibits and divides.

result.statement: If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment.
result.proof:
Let AB be a straight line cut at random at the point C. I say that the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with the square on CB.

**Step 1.** On CB describe the square CDEB [1.46], with CD and BE the sides standing on CB at C and B respectively, and DE the side opposite CB. Since CDEB is a square, its four sides CD, DE, EB, BC are equal to one another and its four angles DCB, CDE, DEB, EBC are right angles [D1.22].

**Step 2.** Since the angles DCB, CBE are right, the straight line CB falling on the two straight lines CD, BE makes the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles; therefore CD is parallel to BE [1.28]. In the same way, since the angles CDE, DCB are right, the straight line CD falling on DE, CB makes the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles; therefore DE is parallel to CB [1.28].

**Step 3.** Produce ED beyond D [P2], and through the point A draw AF parallel to CD [1.31], F being the point in which AF meets ED produced. Since AF is parallel to CD, and CD is parallel to BE (Step 2), AF is also parallel to BE [1.30].

**Step 4.** In the quadrilateral AFEB, AF is parallel to BE (Step 3), and FE, which lies along the straight line DE, is parallel to AB, which lies along the straight line CB (Step 2); therefore AFEB is a parallelogram. Since AF is parallel to BE and AB falls on them, the angles FAB, ABE are together equal to two right angles [1.29]; but the angle ABE is the angle EBC of the square, which is right (Step 1); therefore the angle FAB is right. Likewise FE falls on the parallels AF, BE, so the angles AFE, FEB are together equal to two right angles [1.29]; the angle FEB is the angle DEB of the square, which is right (Step 1); therefore the angle AFE is right. Thus AFEB is a rectangular parallelogram, namely the rectangle contained by AB, BE [D2.1]; call it AE.

**Step 5.** In the quadrilateral ACDF, AF is parallel to CD (Step 3), and FD, which lies along ED, is parallel to AC, which lies along CB (Step 2); therefore ACDF is a parallelogram. Since AF is parallel to CD and AC falls on them, the angles FAC, ACD are together equal to two right angles [1.29]; but the angle FAC is the angle FAB, which is right (Step 4); therefore the angle ACD is right. Thus ACDF is a rectangular parallelogram, namely the rectangle contained by AC, CD [D2.1]; call it AD. Call the square CDEB also CE.

**Step 6.** The straight line CD divides the figure AE into the two figures AD and CE, and AE is made up of these two parts; therefore AE is equal to AD together with CE.

**Step 7.** Now AE is the rectangle contained by AB, BE (Step 4), and BE is equal to BC (Step 1); therefore AE is the rectangle contained by AB, BC. Again, AD is the rectangle contained by AC, CD (Step 5), and CD is equal to CB (Step 1); therefore AD is the rectangle contained by AC, CB. And CE is the square described on CB (Step 1).

**Step 8.** Therefore, by Step 6, the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with the square on CB. Therefore, if a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment. Q.E.D.

**USED:** 1.46, D1.22, 1.28, P2, 1.31, 1.30, 1.29, D2.1

result.statement: If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole is equal to the squares on the segments and twice the rectangle contained by the segments.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the straight line, cut at random at the point C. I say that the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB. On AB describe the square ADEB [1.46], and join DB [P1].

**Step 2.** Since ADEB is a square, it is right-angled [D1.22]; so the straight line AB, falling on AD and BE, makes the interior angles DAB, ABE on the same side equal to two right angles, and therefore AD is parallel to BE [1.28]. In the same way, since the angles ADE, DAB are right, DE is parallel to AB [1.28].

**Step 3.** Through C draw CF parallel to AD, meeting DB at G and DE at F; and through G draw HK parallel to AB, meeting AD at H and BE at K [1.31]. Since CF is parallel to AD and AD to BE, CF is also parallel to BE; and since HK is parallel to AB and AB to DE, HK is also parallel to DE [1.30]. Consequently AHGC, CGKB, HDFG and GFEK are all parallelograms, and ADEB is a parallelogram with diameter DB.

**Step 4.** Since CF is parallel to AD and the straight line DB falls on them, the exterior angle CGB is equal to the interior and opposite angle ADB [1.29].

**Step 5.** Since ADEB is a square, BA is equal to AD [D1.22]; so in the triangle ABD the angle ADB is equal to the angle ABD [1.5]. Therefore the angle CGB is also equal to the angle CBG [CN1].

**Step 6.** In the triangle CGB the angle CGB is equal to the angle CBG; therefore the side CB, which subtends the angle CGB, is equal to the side CG, which subtends the angle CBG [1.6].

**Step 7.** CGKB is a parallelogram (Step 3); therefore its opposite sides are equal, CB to GK and CG to KB [1.34]. But CB is equal to CG (Step 6); therefore the four sides CB, CG, GK, KB are all equal to one another [CN1], and CGKB is equilateral.

**Step 8.** Since CG is parallel to BK and the straight line CB falls on them, the interior angles GCB, CBK on the same side are equal to two right angles [1.29]. But the angle CBK is right, being an angle of the square ADEB [D1.22]; therefore the angle GCB is also right. And the opposite angles of the parallelogram CGKB are equal [1.34], so the angles CGK, GKB are likewise right. Thus CGKB is both equilateral and right-angled, that is, a square [D1.22]; and it is the square described on CB.

**Step 9.** Similarly HDFG is a square. For, HK being parallel to AB and DB falling on them, the exterior angle DGH is equal to the interior and opposite angle DBA [1.29], which is equal to the angle GDH (Step 5) [CN1]; hence HD is equal to HG [1.6]. Since HDFG is a parallelogram, HD is equal to GF and HG to DF [1.34], so that HDFG is equilateral [CN1]. Also the angle HDF is right [D1.22]; DF being parallel to HG and DH falling on them, the angles HDF, DHG are equal to two right angles [1.29], so the angle DHG is right; and the opposite angles of the parallelogram are equal [1.34], so HDFG is right-angled. Hence HDFG is a square [D1.22]. Moreover HG is equal to AC, being opposite sides of the parallelogram AHGC [1.34]; so HDFG is the square on AC.

**Step 10.** Next, AHGC is a parallelogram, and since CF is parallel to AD and AB falls on them, the angles DAC, ACG are equal to two right angles [1.29]; the angle DAC is right [D1.22], so the angle ACG is right, and AHGC is a rectangular parallelogram. Hence AG is the rectangle contained by AC and CG [D2.1]; and CG is equal to CB (Step 6); therefore AG is equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB.

**Step 11.** In the parallelogram ADEB with diameter DB, HF and CK are the parallelograms about the diameter and AG, GE are their complements; therefore AG is equal to GE [1.43]. Hence GE is also equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB, and AG together with GE is twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB [CN2].

**Step 12.** Now HF is the square on AC and CK is the square on CB (Steps 8, 9), while AG and GE together are twice the rectangle AC, CB (Step 11). Adding these equals, HF, CK, AG, GE together are equal to the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB [CN2]. But HF, CK, AG, GE together make up the whole figure ADEB, which is the square on AB. Therefore the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB and twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB. QED.

result.statement: If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half.
result.proof:
## Proposition 2.5
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut into equal segments at C, so that AC = CB, and into unequal segments at D, so that AD is not equal to DB; then D is a point of AB other than C. If D lies between A and C, interchange the names of A and B; so we may suppose that D lies between C and B. We must show that the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CD is equal to the square on CB.

**Step 2.** On CB describe the square CEFB [1.46], with CE and BF the sides at right angles to CB and EF the side opposite to CB; by the construction of 1.46, CE is parallel to BF and CB is parallel to EF. Join BE [P1]; BE is a diameter of the square CEFB.

**Step 3.** Through D draw DG parallel to CE [1.31]. Since D lies between C and B, DG runs across the square from the side CB to the side EF and cuts the diameter BE; let H be the point where DG cuts BE, and G the point where it meets EF. Through H draw the straight line KM parallel to AB [1.31], meeting CE at L and BF at M. Through A draw AK parallel to CE [1.31], meeting KM at K.

**Step 4.** By construction DG and AK are parallel to CE, and KM is parallel to AB, while CE and BF are at right angles to CB; hence the quadrilaterals CDHL, DBMH, LHGE, HMFG, ACLK and ADHK cut off in the figure are all parallelograms, and their angles, like those of the square, are right angles. In the square CEFB with diameter BE, the parallelograms DBMH (call it DM) and LHGE (call it LG) are the parallelograms about the diameter, since their diameters HB and HE lie along BE; and CDHL (call it CH) and HMFG (call it HF) are their complements.

**Step 5.** Since CH and HF are the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter BE of the parallelogram CEFB, the complement CH is equal to the complement HF [1.43].

**Step 6.** Add the parallelogram DM to each. CH together with DM is the whole parallelogram CBML (call it CM), and HF together with DM is the whole parallelogram DBFG (call it DF). Therefore CM = DF [CN2].

**Step 7.** The parallelograms ACLK (call it AL) and CBML (that is, CM) stand on the equal bases AC, CB and lie in the same parallels AB, KM. Therefore AL = CM [1.36].

**Step 8.** Since AL = CM and CM = DF, AL = DF [CN1].

**Step 9.** Add CH to each. AL together with CH is the whole parallelogram ADHK (call it AH). DF together with CH consists of the parallelogram DM about the diameter together with its two complements CH and HF, which is a gnomon [D2.2]; call it the gnomon NOP. It is the square CEFB with LG removed. Therefore AH = gnomon NOP [CN2].

**Step 10.** DM is a parallelogram about the diameter BE of the square CEFB; therefore DM is itself a square [2.4, Porism: in square areas the parallelograms about the diameter are squares]. A square is equilateral [D1.22]; hence DH = DB.

**Step 11.** AH is a rectangular parallelogram whose right angle at D is contained by AD and DH; so AH is the rectangle contained by AD, DH [D2.1]. Since DH = DB, AH is the rectangle contained by AD, DB. Consequently, by Step 9, the gnomon NOP is equal to the rectangle contained by AD, DB.

**Step 12.** LG is also a parallelogram about the diameter BE of the square CEFB, so LG is a square [2.4, Porism]. Its side LH is equal to CD, because CD and LH are opposite sides of the parallelogram CH [1.34]. Therefore LG is a square described on a straight line equal to CD, that is, LG is equal to the square on CD.

**Step 13.** Add LG to each of the equals in Step 11. Then the gnomon NOP together with LG is equal to the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CD [CN2].

**Step 14.** But the gnomon NOP together with LG is the whole square CEFB, which is the square described on CB. Therefore the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CD is equal to the square on CB [CN1].

Therefore, if a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, CN1, CN2, D1.22, D2.1, D2.2, 1.31, 1.34, 1.36, 1.43, 1.46, 2.4

result.statement: If a straight line be bisected and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line and the added straight line together with the square on the half is equal to the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line.
result.proof:
## Proposition 2.6
**Statement:** If a straight line be bisected and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line and the added straight line together with the square on the half is equal to the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be bisected at C, so that AC = CB, and let the straight line BD be added to it in a straight line, so that A, C, B, D lie in this order on the single straight line AD. It is required to prove that the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CB is equal to the square on CD.

**Step 2.** On CD describe the square CEFD [1.46], CE and DF being the sides drawn at right angles to CD and EF the side opposite to CD, and join DE [P1]. By its construction in 1.46 the square has its opposite sides parallel, CE ∥ DF and CD ∥ EF, so CEFD is a parallelogram with DE as a diameter; and all its sides are equal and all its angles are right [D1.22].

**Step 3.** Through B draw BG parallel to CE [1.31], meeting the diameter DE at H and the side EF at G; through H draw KM parallel to AD [1.31], meeting CE at L and DF at M; and through A draw AK parallel to DM [1.31], meeting KM at K.

**Step 4.** Since BG ∥ CE and CE ∥ DF, also BG ∥ DF; since AK ∥ DM and DM ∥ CE, also AK ∥ CE; and since KM ∥ AD and AD ∥ EF, also KM ∥ EF [1.30]. Hence each of the figures AL (= AKLC), CH (= CLHB), BM (= BHMD), LG (= LEGH), HF (= HGFM), CM (= CLMD) and AM (= AKMD) has its opposite sides parallel and is a parallelogram. Because H lies on the diameter DE, LG and BM are the parallelograms about the diameter DE of the parallelogram CEFD, and CH, HF are their complements; the parallelogram BM together with the two complements CH, HF is a gnomon [D2.2], which we call the gnomon NOP. The gnomon NOP together with LG makes up the whole square CEFD.

**Step 5.** Since AC = CB, the parallelograms AL and CH are on the equal bases AC, CB and in the same parallels AD, KM; therefore AL = CH [1.36].

**Step 6.** Since CH and HF are the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter DE of the parallelogram CEFD, CH = HF [1.43].

**Step 7.** Therefore AL = HF [CN1].

**Step 8.** Let CM be added to each. AL together with CM is the whole parallelogram AM, and HF together with CM (which is made up of CH and BM) is the gnomon NOP. Therefore AM = gnomon NOP [CN2].

**Step 9.** Now BM is a parallelogram about the diameter of the square CEFD; hence BM is itself a square [2.4, Porism], so that DM = DB [D1.22]. Further, AM is a parallelogram whose angle ADM is the angle CDF of the square and is therefore right [D1.22]; since AK ∥ DM and AD falls on them, the angle KAD together with the angle ADM equals two right angles [1.29], so KAD is right; and the angles AKM, KMD, being opposite to ADM, KAD in the parallelogram AM, are also right [1.34]. Thus AM is a rectangular parallelogram, namely the rectangle contained by AD, DM [D2.1]; and since DM = DB, AM is the rectangle contained by AD, DB.

**Step 10.** Therefore the gnomon NOP is equal to the rectangle contained by AD, DB [CN1].

**Step 11.** Again, LG is a parallelogram about the diameter of the square CEFD, so LG is a square [2.4, Porism]; and its side LH is equal to CB, these being opposite sides of the parallelogram CH [1.34]. Therefore LG is the square on a straight line equal to CB, that is, LG is equal to the square on CB.

**Step 12.** Let LG be added to each. Then the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CB is equal to the gnomon NOP together with LG [CN2]. But the gnomon NOP together with LG is the whole square CEFD, which is the square described on CD. Therefore the rectangle contained by AD, DB together with the square on CB is equal to the square on CD [CN1]. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, CN1, CN2, D1.22, D2.1, D2.2, 1.29, 1.30, 1.31, 1.34, 1.36, 1.43, 1.46, 2.4

Path note: For DM = DB and for LG being a square, the most direct route is the Porism to 2.4 (in a square the parallelograms about the diameter are squares); the same facts could be derived at greater length from the angle theorems of Book 1 alone, but that longer route was not taken.

result.statement: If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole and that on one of the segments both together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole and the said segment and the square on the remaining segment.
result.proof:
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole and that on one of the segments both together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole and the said segment and the square on the remaining segment.

Let the straight line AB be cut at random at the point C. I say that the squares on AB, BC are together equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC together with the square on CA.

**Step 1.** Since the straight line AB has been cut at random at C, the square on the whole AB is equal to the squares on the segments AC, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB [2.4].

**Step 2.** Again, since AB has been cut at random at C, the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BC is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments AC, CB together with the square on BC [2.3].

**Step 3.** Adding the equals of Step 2 to themselves, twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AC, CB together with twice the square on BC [CN2].

**Step 4.** Let the square on AC be added to each; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB, twice the square on BC, and the square on AC taken together [CN2].

**Step 5.** But, by Step 1, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC, CB together with twice the rectangle AC, CB; let the square on BC be added to each; therefore the square on AB together with the square on BC is equal to twice the rectangle AC, CB, twice the square on BC, and the square on AC taken together [CN2].

**Step 6.** Now the two magnitudes obtained in Steps 4 and 5, namely twice the rectangle AB, BC together with the square on AC, and the squares on AB, BC taken together, are each equal to the same thing, namely twice the rectangle AC, CB, twice the square on BC, and the square on AC taken together; therefore they are equal to one another [CN1].

**Step 7.** Therefore the square on the whole AB and the square on the segment BC are together equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BC together with the square on the remaining segment AC. Q.E.D.

**Path note.** A geometric route also exists: describe the square on AB [1.46], draw the diameter and the two parallels through C as in the figure of 2.4, and apply 1.43 to the complements, adding the square on CB to each and then the square on AC. That route requires re-establishing that the parallelograms about the diameter are the squares on CB and AC. The route above, which obtains the result directly from the decomposition already proved in 2.4 and the rectangle identity of 2.3, is the more direct and is the one adopted.

result.statement: If a straight line be cut at random, four times the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments together with the square on the remaining segment is equal to the square described on the whole and the aforesaid segment as on one straight line.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut at random at the point C. Produce AB in a straight line beyond B [P2], and on the produced part let BD be made equal to CB [1.3]. Then AD is the straight line made up of the whole AB and the segment BC placed as on one straight line, so that the square on AD is the square described on the whole and the aforesaid segment as on one straight line. It is to be proved that four times the rectangle contained by AB, BC together with the square on AC is equal to the square on AD.

**Step 2.** The straight line AD is cut at the point B. Therefore, by 2.4, the square on AD is equal to the squares on AB, BD together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, BD.

**Step 3.** Since BD is equal to CB, the square on BD is a square described on a straight line equal to CB, that is, it is the square on CB; and the rectangle contained by AB, BD, being the rectangle contained by AB and a straight line equal to CB, is the rectangle contained by AB, CB, a rectangle being that which is contained by the two straight lines about its right angle [D2.1]. Hence, from Step 2, the square on AD is equal to the squares on AB, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB.

**Step 4.** Again, the straight line AB is cut at C. Therefore, by 2.7, the squares on AB, CB together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB together with the square on AC.

**Step 5.** Let twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB be added to each of these equals. Then the squares on AB, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB are equal to four times the rectangle contained by AB, CB together with the square on AC [CN2].

**Step 6.** But the squares on AB, CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AB, CB were shown in Step 3 to be equal to the square on AD. Therefore, things equal to the same thing being equal to one another [CN1], the square on AD is equal to four times the rectangle contained by AB, CB together with the square on AC.

**Step 7.** Therefore four times the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BC, together with the square on the remaining segment AC, is equal to the square on AD, which is the square described on the whole and the aforesaid segment as on one straight line. Q.E.D.

Path note: the result can also be reached by describing the square on AD and dissecting it by parallels into squares and complements (the gnomon method used in 2.4-2.7); the route through 2.4 and 2.7 is the most direct from the preceding theorems and is chosen for that reason.

result.statement: If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the squares on the unequal segments of the whole are double of the square on the half and of the square on the straight line between the points of section.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be cut into equal segments at C and into unequal segments at D, so that AC = CB, and let D lie between C and B. It is to be proved that the squares on AD, DB together are double of the squares on AC, CD together.

**Step 2.** From C draw CE at right angles to AB (1.11); produce it as far as needed (P2) and cut off CE equal to AC (1.3), so that CE is also equal to CB (CN1). Join EA and EB (P1).

**Step 3.** Through D draw DF parallel to CE (1.31), meeting EB at F; through F draw FG parallel to AB (1.31), meeting CE at G. Join AF (P1).

**Step 4.** Since CA = CE, the angle EAC is equal to the angle AEC (1.5). Since CE stands at right angles to AB, the angles ACE and ECB are right (D1.10). In the triangle ACE the three angles are together equal to two right angles (1.32); the angle ACE being right, the remaining angles AEC, EAC are together equal to one right angle (CN3). Being equal to one another, each of them is half a right angle.

**Step 5.** In the same way, since CB = CE, in the triangle ECB the angles CEB, EBC are equal (1.5), and together they are equal to one right angle (1.32, CN3); so each of them is half a right angle.

**Step 6.** Therefore the whole angle AEB, made up of the angles AEC and CEB, each half a right angle, is a right angle.

**Step 7.** Since GF is parallel to CB and the straight line EC falls upon them, the exterior angle EGF is equal to the interior and opposite angle ECB (1.29), which is right; so the angle EGF is right. The angle GEF is the same as the angle CEB, which is half a right angle (Step 5). Hence in the triangle EGF the remaining angle EFG is half a right angle (1.32, CN3), so that the angle GEF is equal to the angle EFG, and therefore the side GE is equal to the side GF (1.6).

**Step 8.** Since DF is parallel to CE and the straight line AB falls upon them, the exterior angle FDB is equal to the interior and opposite angle ECD (1.29), which is right; so the angle FDB is right. The angle DBF is the same as the angle EBC, which is half a right angle (Step 5). Hence in the triangle DFB the remaining angle DFB is half a right angle (1.32, CN3), so that the angle DFB is equal to the angle DBF, and therefore the side DF is equal to the side DB (1.6).

**Step 9.** Since AC = CE, the square on AC is equal to the square on CE; hence the squares on AC, CE together are double of the square on AC. But the angle ACE is right, so the square on EA is equal to the squares on AC, CE (1.47). Therefore the square on EA is double of the square on AC (CN1).

**Step 10.** Since EG = GF (Step 7), the square on EG is equal to the square on GF; hence the squares on EG, GF together are double of the square on GF. But the angle EGF is right (Step 7), so the square on EF is equal to the squares on EG, GF (1.47). Therefore the square on EF is double of the square on GF (CN1). Now CG is parallel to DF and GF is parallel to CD, so CDFG is a parallelogram, and its opposite sides GF, CD are equal (1.34). Therefore the square on EF is double of the square on CD.

**Step 11.** Adding these results, the squares on AE, EF together are double of the squares on AC, CD together (CN2).

**Step 12.** But the angle AEF is right (Step 6), so the square on AF is equal to the squares on AE, EF (1.47). Therefore the square on AF is double of the squares on AC, CD together (CN1).

**Step 13.** Since the angle FDB is right (Step 8), and the adjacent angles ADF, FDB are together equal to two right angles (1.13), the angle ADF is also right (CN3). Therefore the square on AF is equal to the squares on AD, DF (1.47).

**Step 14.** And DF = DB (Step 8), so the square on DF is equal to the square on DB; hence the squares on AD, DF together are equal to the squares on AD, DB together (CN2), and so the squares on AD, DB together are equal to the square on AF (CN1). Therefore the squares on AD, DB together are double of the squares on AC, CD together (CN1).

**Step 15.** Therefore, if a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the squares on the unequal segments of the whole are double of the square on the half and of the square on the straight line between the points of section. Q.E.D.

result.statement: If a straight line be bisected, and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the square on the whole with the added straight line and the square on the added straight line both together are double of the square on the half and of the square described on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line as on one straight line.
result.proof:
**Statement:** If a straight line be bisected, and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the square on the whole with the added straight line and the square on the added straight line both together are double of the square on the half and of the square described on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line as on one straight line.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be bisected at C, and let the straight line BD be added to it in a straight line, so that A, C, B, D lie in order on one straight line. We must show that the squares on AD and DB together are double of the squares on AC and CD together.

**Step 2.** From the point C draw CE at right angles to AB [1.11], and cut off CE equal to AC, and hence equal to CB, since AC = CB [1.3]. Join EA and EB [P1].

**Step 3.** Through E draw EF parallel to AD, and through D draw FD parallel to CE [1.31]; let these meet at F. Then ECDF is a parallelogram, its opposite sides EF, CD and EC, FD being parallel.

**Step 4.** Since the straight line EF falls upon the parallel straight lines EC and FD, the interior angles on the same side, CEF and EFD, are together equal to two right angles [1.29]. The angle FEB is a part of the angle FEC, so it is less than the angle FEC [CN5]. Therefore the angles FEB and EFD together are less than two right angles.

**Step 5.** Hence EB and FD, if produced in the direction of B and D [P2], will meet on that side [P5]. Let them be produced and meet at G, and join AG [P1].

**Step 6.** Since AC = CE, the angle EAC is equal to the angle AEC [1.5]. The angle ACE is right, so, since the three angles of the triangle ACE are together equal to two right angles [1.32], the remaining angles AEC and EAC together are equal to one right angle [CN3]. Being equal, each of them is half a right angle.

**Step 7.** In the same way, since CE = CB, the angle CEB is equal to the angle CBE [1.5], and the angle ECB is right, so each of the angles CEB and EBC is half a right angle [1.32, CN3]. Therefore the whole angle AEB, being made up of the halves AEC and CEB, is a right angle [CN2].

**Step 8.** The angle EBC is half a right angle; and the angle DBG is equal to the angle EBC, since they are vertical angles formed by the straight lines EG and AD crossing at B [1.15]. Therefore the angle DBG is half a right angle.

**Step 9.** The straight line CD falls upon the parallel straight lines CE and DG, so the alternate angles ECD and BDG are equal [1.29]. The angle ECD is right; therefore the angle BDG is right.

**Step 10.** In the triangle BDG, the angles BDG and DBG together with the angle DGB are equal to two right angles [1.32]; since BDG is right and DBG is half a right angle, the remaining angle DGB is half a right angle [CN3]. Therefore the angle DGB is equal to the angle DBG, and so the side BD is equal to the side GD [1.6].

**Step 11.** Since ECDF is a parallelogram, the angle EFD is equal to the opposite angle ECD [1.34], and so the angle EFD is right; and since G lies on FD produced, the angle EFG is this same right angle. The angle EGF is the same as the angle DGB, so it is half a right angle. Hence in the triangle EFG the remaining angle FEG is half a right angle [1.32, CN3]. Therefore the angle FEG is equal to the angle EGF, and so the side GF is equal to the side EF [1.6].

**Step 12.** Since EC = CA, the square on EC is equal to the square on CA; therefore the squares on EC and CA together are double of the square on CA. But the angle ECA is right, so the square on EA is equal to the squares on EC and CA together [1.47]. Therefore the square on EA is double of the square on AC [CN1].

**Step 13.** Since GF = EF, the square on GF is equal to the square on EF; therefore the squares on GF and FE together are double of the square on EF. But the angle EFG is right, so the square on EG is equal to the squares on GF and FE together [1.47]. Therefore the square on EG is double of the square on EF [CN1]. Also EF is equal to the opposite side CD of the parallelogram ECDF [1.34]; therefore the square on EG is double of the square on CD.

**Step 14.** The angle AEG is right (Step 7), so the square on AG is equal to the squares on AE and EG together [1.47]. By Steps 12 and 13, the squares on AE and EG together are double of the square on AC together with double of the square on CD [CN2]. Therefore the square on AG is double of the squares on AC and CD together [CN1].

**Step 15.** The angle ADG is right (Step 9), so the square on AG is also equal to the squares on AD and DG together [1.47]. But DG = DB (Step 10), so the square on DG is equal to the square on DB, and hence the square on AG is equal to the squares on AD and DB together [CN1].

**Step 16.** Therefore the squares on AD and DB together are equal to the square on AG, which is double of the squares on AC and CD together [CN1]. That is, the square on the whole with the added straight line, AD, together with the square on the added straight line, DB, is double of the square on the half, AC, together with the square on CD, the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P1, P2, P5, CN1, CN2, CN3, CN5, 1.3, 1.5, 1.6, 1.11, 1.15, 1.29, 1.31, 1.32, 1.34, 1.47

result.statement: To cut a given straight line so that the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the square on the remaining segment.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line. On AB describe the square ABDC [1.46]; its four sides are equal and its angles are right [D1.22].

**Step 2.** Bisect AC at the point E [1.10], and join BE [P1].

**Step 3.** Produce CA in a straight line through A to F [P2], and on the produced line cut off EF equal to EB [1.3].

**Step 4.** On AF describe the square AFGH [1.46]. Since the angle BAC is right and F lies on CA produced, the adjacent angle BAF is also right [1.13]; hence the side AH of the square AFGH, which stands at right angles to AF at A, lies along AB, so that H is a point of AB.

**Step 5.** Produce GH to meet CD at K [P2]. Then FCKG (call it FK) is a rectangle with sides CF and FG, and AHKC (call it AK) is a rectangle with sides AH and AC, common to FK and to the square AD.

**Step 6.** The straight line AC has been bisected at E, and the straight line AF has been added to it in a straight line. Therefore the rectangle contained by CF and FA together with the square on AE is equal to the square on EF [2.6].

**Step 7.** But EF is equal to EB (Step 3), so the square on EF is equal to the square on EB. Hence the rectangle CF·FA together with the square on AE is equal to the square on EB.

**Step 8.** Since the angle EAB, which is the angle CAB of the square, is right, in the right-angled triangle EAB the square on EB is equal to the squares on BA and AE together [1.47].

**Step 9.** Therefore the rectangle CF·FA together with the square on AE is equal to the squares on BA and AE together [CN1].

**Step 10.** Subtract the square on AE from each; the remainders are equal [CN3]. Therefore the rectangle CF·FA is equal to the square on AB.

**Step 11.** Now the rectangle CF·FA is the rectangle FK, for FG is equal to FA (sides of the square AFGH) and the angle at F is right, so that FK is contained by CF and FG [D2.1]. And the square on AB is the square AD. Therefore FK is equal to AD [CN1].

**Step 12.** From each subtract the rectangle AK, which is common to both; the remainders are equal [CN3]. Therefore the remainder FH, the square AFGH, is equal to the remainder HD, the rectangle HBDK.

**Step 13.** But HD is the rectangle contained by AB and BH, since BD is equal to AB (sides of the square ABDC) and the angle at B is right [D2.1]; and FH is the square on AH.

**Step 14.** Therefore the rectangle contained by AB and BH is equal to the square on AH [CN1]. Thus the given straight line AB has been cut at H so that the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment BH is equal to the square on the remaining segment AH. Q.E.F.

result.statement: In obtuse-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, namely that on which the   perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be an obtuse-angled triangle having the angle BAC obtuse. Produce CA beyond A (P2), and from the point B draw BD perpendicular to CA produced (1.12), meeting it at D. Since BD is a perpendicular, the angles BDC and BDA are right (D1.10).

**Step 2.** The foot D lies on CA produced beyond A, that is, outside the triangle on the side of the obtuse angle. For if D coincided with A, the angle BAC would be right, whereas it is obtuse, i.e. greater than a right angle (D1.11); and if D lay on CA itself or on AC produced beyond C, then in the triangle BAD the angle BDA would be right and the angle BAD would be the obtuse angle BAC itself, so that two angles of the triangle BAD would together not be less than two right angles, contrary to 1.17. Hence D falls beyond A, CD is one straight line cut at the point A, and AD is the straight line cut off outside the triangle by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.

**Step 3.** Since the straight line CD has been cut at random at the point A, the square on DC is equal to the squares on CA, AD and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD (2.4).

**Step 4.** Let the square on DB be added to each (CN2); therefore the squares on CD, DB are equal to the squares on CA, AD, DB and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD.

**Step 5.** Since the angle BDC is right, the triangle BDC is right-angled, so the square on CB is equal to the squares on CD, DB (1.47); and likewise, since the angle BDA is right, the square on AB is equal to the squares on AD, DB (1.47).

**Step 6.** Therefore the square on CB, being equal to the squares on CD, DB (Step 5), is equal to the squares on CA, AD, DB and twice the rectangle CA, AD (Step 4, CN1); and since the squares on AD, DB are together equal to the square on AB (Step 5), the square on CB is equal to the squares on CA, AB and twice the rectangle contained by CA, AD (CN1).

**Step 7.** Hence the square on CB, the side subtending the obtuse angle, is greater than the squares on CA, AB, the sides containing the obtuse angle, by twice the rectangle contained by CA, the side on which the perpendicular falls, and AD, the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle. Q.E.D.

**USED:** P2, 1.12, D1.10, D1.11, 1.17, 2.4, CN2, 1.47, CN1

result.statement: In acute-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the acute angle is less than the squares on the sides containing the acute angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the acute angle, namely that on which the perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off within by the perpendicular towards the acute angle.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let ABC be an acute-angled triangle, so that each of its angles ABC, BCA, CAB is acute (D1.21), that is, less than a right angle (D1.12). Produce BC indefinitely in both directions (P2), and from the point A draw AD perpendicular to the straight line BC (1.12); then the angles ADB, ADC are right (D1.10).

**Step 2.** The foot D lies within BC. For suppose D fell on BC produced beyond B. Then angle ABC would be an exterior angle of triangle ABD, and so greater than the interior and opposite angle ADB (1.16), which is right; since all right angles are equal (P4), angle ABC would be greater than a right angle and hence not acute (D1.12), contrary to hypothesis. If D coincided with B, angle ABC would itself be a right angle (D1.10), again contrary to hypothesis. The same reasoning applied to the acute angle ACB shows that D neither falls beyond C nor coincides with C. Therefore D lies between B and C, so that the straight line BC is cut at the point D into the segments BD, DC.

**Step 3.** Since the straight line BC has been cut at D, the square on BC together with the square on BD is equal to twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD together with the square on DC (2.7).

**Step 4.** Let the square on AD be added to each; then the squares on BC, BD, AD are together equal to twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD together with the squares on DC, AD (CN2).

**Step 5.** Since the angle ADB is right, the square on AB is equal to the squares on BD, AD (1.47); and since the angle ADC is right, the square on AC is equal to the squares on DC, AD (1.47).

**Step 6.** Substituting these equalities into Step 4, the squares on BC, AB are together equal to twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD together with the square on AC (CN1).

**Step 7.** Subtracting twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD from each side, the square on AC is equal to the squares on BC, AB less twice the rectangle contained by BC, BD (CN3). That is, the square on AC, the side subtending the acute angle ABC, is less than the squares on the sides AB, BC containing that angle by twice the rectangle contained by BC, the side on which the perpendicular falls, and BD, the straight line cut off within by the perpendicular towards the acute angle. Q.E.D.

result.statement: To construct a square equal to a given rectilineal figure.
result.proof:
**Step 1.** Let A be the given rectilineal figure. Draw a right angle [1.11], and in this right angle construct the parallelogram BD equal to the rectilineal figure A [1.45]; BD is thus a rectangular parallelogram with the right angle at E, contained by the two sides BE, ED [D2.1].

**Step 2.** If BE is equal to ED, then, since the opposite sides of the parallelogram BD are equal [1.34], BD is equilateral; and it is right-angled; therefore BD is a square [D1.22], and what was required has been done.

**Step 3.** If not, one of BE, ED is greater. Let BE be the greater. Produce BE in a straight line to F [P2], and cut off EF equal to ED [1.3].

**Step 4.** Bisect BF at the point G [1.10]. With centre G and distance GF describe a circle [P3]; since GB is equal to GF, the point B also lies on the circumference.

**Step 5.** From the point E draw EH at right angles to BF [1.11], and let it meet the circumference of the circle at H. Join GH [P1].

**Step 6.** Since the straight line BF has been cut into equal segments at G and into unequal segments at E, the rectangle contained by BE, EF together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GF [2.5].

**Step 7.** But GF is equal to GH, both being straight lines drawn from the centre G to the circumference [D1.15]; therefore the square on GF is the square on GH, and so the rectangle contained by BE, EF together with the square on EG is equal to the square on GH.

**Step 8.** Since the angle HEG is right, the square on GH is equal to the squares on HE, EG [1.47].

**Step 9.** Therefore the rectangle contained by BE, EF together with the square on EG is equal to the squares on HE, EG, each being equal to the square on GH [CN1].

**Step 10.** Let the square on EG be subtracted from each; then the remaining rectangle contained by BE, EF is equal to the square on EH [CN3].

**Step 11.** But EF is equal to ED; therefore the rectangle contained by BE, EF is the rectangle contained by BE, ED, which is the parallelogram BD [D2.1]. Therefore BD is equal to the square on EH.

**Step 12.** And BD is equal to the rectilineal figure A; therefore the rectilineal figure A is also equal to the square on EH [CN1].

**Step 13.** On EH describe the square [1.46]; this square is equal to the given rectilineal figure A. Therefore a square has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal figure A. Q.E.F.

*Path note:* the perpendicular EH is drawn directly by 1.11 (the more direct route) rather than by producing DE to the circumference, which would additionally require 1.13 to establish that the angle at E is right.
